articles.title_orig: Donald Trump lands in China for unprecedented meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump lands in China for unprecedented meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump has arrived in Shenzhen ahead of an unprecedented trilateral sit-down with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin
The three leaders are attending a summit of Asia Pacific leaders hosted by China. Xi earlier welcomed Putin whom he called an "old friend"
Xi is striking a delicate balance as they discuss the war in Ukraine, energy supplies and their ties to the US, writes our China correspondent
Some Russian newspapers are already calling it a "diplomatic victory" for Putin - simply because it's happening, writes our Russia editor
Trump flew into China from the Philippines, where he was attending another summit - images show him meeting India's Narendra Modi, Australia's Anthony Albanese and Japan's Sanae Takaichi
Trump said a US-Philippines trade deal was "consummated" but gave no details - the whirlwind visit left little time for in-depth discussions, writes our South East Asia correspondent
Edited by Gavin Butler with reporting from Laura Bicker, Steve Rosenberg and Stephen McDonell in Shenzhen and Nada Tawfik travelling with President Trump
President Xi Jinping hugs President Donald Trump as the US leader steps off his plane in Shenzhen.
The red carpet was rolled out for Trump's arrival.
Some local residents are gathering outside the hotel where President Donald Trump is reportedly staying.
A heavy police presence is on the scene, with officers urging passers-by to not linger.
The hotel entrance is blocked off by barricades.
Laura Bicker Reporting from Shenzhen
Others said they wanted to make Trump feel welcome.
But itâs not just world leaders the people of Shenzhen are keen to meet.
Many foreign journalists, including our BBC teams, have found themselves embraced by local people eager to say hello. It is rare for people here to meet a Western journalist as there are so few in China.
There is also a sense of excitement in the parks and on the streets that this city of 18 million people has been chosen to host such an historic moment.
Shenzhen residents gathering to catch a glimpse of Trump
Small groups of people from Shenzhen have gathered along the route of Donald Trumpâs motorcade to welcome the US president.
Security and surveillance in parts of the city have ramped up in the last few hours, in preparation for the unprecedented summit between all three of the worldâs most powerful men.
âI hope Mr Trump coming here can be a bridge between the US and China,â one young man told us as he waited on a street corner near the US presidentâs hotel.
Earlier, some residents were taking photographs as Air Force One was about to touch down in Shenzhen
Trump's plane has just touched down in Shenzhen. Stay with us for more updates of his arrival.
We're getting some updates from Chinese state media on Xi's earlier meeting with Putin. The Chinese leader described relations between Beijing and Moscow as "stable as a mountain, unshaken by storms".
The relationship between both countries has "provided greater stability and certainty to a world fraught with turmoil and upheaval", Xi said, according to China's Xinhua News Agency.
Xi also urged both states to strengthen cooperation and explore new areas of collaboration.
As we reported earlier, Xi and Putin largely echoed each other's remarks and hailed bilateral ties.
The trilateral meeting: All eyes will be on Thursday's unprecedented gathering between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Trade tensions: Trump's tariffs have upended global trade order, and China has responded by choking off vital exports like rare earths. A delicate truce on the trade war is set to expire in January.
AI and chips: AI chips are at the centre of a heated US-China tech race. The recent Nvidia scandal has triggered scrutiny on the alleged smuggling of chips to China, which the US says is a national security issue.
Denuclearisation: Trump said talks with Putin and Xi would cover "a lot of things including denuclearisation". But China has long been reluctant to participate in nuclear disarmament talks, citing the disparity between its arsenal and those of the US and Russia.
The war in Ukraine: Experts think a breakthrough is unlikely, due to a tangle of conflicting interests and the lack of Ukraine's participation. US officials have reportedly said Trump was unlikely to broach the topic with Putin and Xi.
The Iran war: Trump has signalled his intention to discuss the Iran war at the trilateral. Moscow and Beijing, while not formal allies of Iran, have maintained strategic partnerships with the Islamic Republic.
Osmond Chia Business reporter
Xi Jinping will be meeting Donald Trump for the third time this year.
And while most experts don't expect major breakthroughs in US-China trade relations, the two nations will likely make some effort to stabilise their fragile trade truce.
The steep tariffs threatened by both sides have been suspended until early next year, but Washington this week imposed tougher curbs on semiconductor trade through South East Asia, which China has relied on to rent advanced AI chips.
Tensions between the sides have also grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang resigned following allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Xi's key goal at the Apec summit is to show that the Nvidia scandal and US mid-term results have not undermined US-China relations, Yeling Tan from the Peterson Institute for International Economics says.
Beijing will also want both sides to commit to cooperating and managing conflicts, Tan adds.
There are concerns, particularly in Europe, that the trilateral between Xi, Trump and Putin would mirror the Yalta Conference held in 1945 as World War Two drew to a close.
Yalta, attended by then-US President Franklin D Roosevelt, former British PM Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin, was fiercely criticised for decisions that shaped the futures of smaller nations without their participation.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned against holding a "Yalta 2, 3, or 4, with a redistribution of influence". He also raised fears the meeting could lead to a deal on Ukraine without Kyiv's involvement.
Some political analysts say the US and China will have much to lose if Europe gets sidelined.
"Moscow would certainly welcome that, but for Washington and Beijing, both of which count Europe as a large and vital economic partner, it would be a cost that is neither necessary nor worthwhile," wrote David Abramson and Evgeny Roshchin in a commentary for the Center for European Policy Analysis.
Churchill (left) and Roosevelt (centre) have been criticised for capitulating to Stalin at the Yalta Conference
China's foreign ministry says the trilateral meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin will involve the exchange of "in-depth views" on issues related to "global peace", state media outlet Xinhua reports.
This vague description echoes previous comments from Beijing that the three leaders would discuss "safeguarding world peace".
Key issues loom over bilateral and trilateral ties, including trade tensions, AI, denuclearisation, and the wars in Ukraine and Iran. But what's actually going to be on the table for discussions remain unclear.
One detail worth watching is who will welcome Trump at the tarmac.
Beijing's choice of Chinese official greeting the US president
would be an indication of how much they value his visit.
During Trump's state visit to China in May, the Chinese leadership
sent Vice-President Han Zheng to welcome the US president at the tarmac.
During Xi's state visit to the US in September, Trump took the
unusual step of greeting him personally at the tarmac.
China would certainly want to reciprocate the gesture by sending a
high-ranking member of the Communist Party's Political Bureau to welcome Trump. But it is unlikely that Xi would go to the airport given his tight
schedule.Cai Qi, his de facto chief of staff, would be
the ideal substitute.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Xi and Putin Meet Ahead of Trump’s Arrival in China
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Xi and Putin Meet Ahead of Trump’s Arrival in China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has landed in Shenzhen for historic trilateral talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin.
Trump is in China for the APEC summit, which President Xi opened with calls for free trade and greater cooperation around artificial intelligence.
He said: "We should actively build partnerships for scientific and technological innovation, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence and promote a green and low-carbon transition."
Putin has also addressed the summit , claiming sanctions imposed on Russia have backfired and strengthened his nation.
The much-anticipated meeting between the three world leaders is set to take place on Thursday, with discussions expected to center on the Iran war and Russia's war in Ukraine.
Though expectations for any concrete outcome are low, Trump, Xi and Putin are expected to hold in-depth discussions on issues crucial for world peace and strategic stability, a spokesperson for China's foreign ministry said Wednesday.
North Korean leader Kim Jong-Un could potentially attend the summit, which is a 21-member gathering of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders.
Trump flew in from Manila, Philippines, where he started a three-day visit to Asia and met key regional allies including Japan, India and Australia.
The APEC host city Shenzhen has been dubbed one of China's "Silicon Valleys" and has been a major hub for China's internet and artificial intelligence companies.
The summit offers an opportunity for Beijing to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms "unilateralism and protectionism," with trade, artificial intelligence, and the Middle East conflict expected to dominate the meeting's agenda.
Xi held several bilateral meetings with attending leaders on the sidelines Wednesday, including South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, to discuss trade, commerce and peace on the Korean Peninsula. Earlier this week, Xi also met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Vietnamese President To Lam.
Xi also had met with Putin earlier Wednesday, before Trump's arrival.

Summit in Chinese tech hub Shenzhen set to include highly anticipated meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin
Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit
What is Apec? Explained in 30 seconds
Thanks for tuning into our live blog of the Apec summit currently under way in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.
There is plenty more to come, so don’t go away, but here is a quick summary of what we know so far.
Chinese president Xi Jinping opened the Apec CEO summit on Wednesday with a speech calling for freer trade and greater cooperation around AI . “We should not only eliminate trade and investment barriers... but also promote inclusive and balanced development,” he said. “We should actively build partnerships for scientific and technological innovation, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence and promote a green and low-carbon transition.”
Russian president Vladimir Putin also addressed the summit, speaking after Ukraine destroyed the vital Kerch road bridge linking occupied Crimea to Russia in a major blow to his four-year-old war. Putin followed Xi on stage with a speech that described Western powers as “ former hegemons ”. He said Europe was in a “humiliating decline” and that anti-Russian sanctions imposed ⁠after his invasion of Ukraine had backfired, instead making his country stronger.
Xi and Putin headed into a meeting after their opening addresses, according to Chinese and Russian state media.
The much-anticipated trilateral meeting between US president Donald Trump, Xi and Putin will take place on Thursday. The three men are due to meet on the sidelines and potentially discuss Russia’s war with Ukraine and the US war in Iran, as well as other flashpoints such as trade, ⁠AI and nuclear weapons.
The meeting has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalised spheres of influence , set the stage for world order after the second world war and became shorthand for great power deals imposed on smaller countries.
It is unclear whether North Korean leader Kim Jong-un will attend the talks, but Trump has floated the possibility. On Wednesday US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the US president was willing to engage, but he did not confirm whether a meeting had been set in Shenzhen.
Trump said on Wednesday that the US has just ⁠concluded a “ very big ⁠trade ​deal” with the Philippines , but he did not provide any details, and Manila ⁠did not announce any agreement. “We’ve just consummated a very big trade deal, the ⁠biggest trade deal we’ve ever made so far, and it ​is a fair ‌deal for both countries,” ‌Trump said during a state luncheon at the Philippine ‌presidential palace. Trump is set to arrive in Shenzhen on Wednesday evening.
While we await Trump to disembark Air Force Once, we have this report from our China correspondent Rebecca Bailey in Shenzhen:
Canada’s Mark Carney has hit back at Vladimir Putin’s earlier assertion that sanctions no longer work in this day and age.
“Mr Putin can ask his financial institutions, he can ask his oligarch friends, he can ask his hockey players whether or not sanctions are a thing of the past. I think he’ll find out that they’re very real, they’re biting,” Carney told reporters.
In his address to the summit this morning, Putin had said that “the traditional tools of economic dominance and de facto coercion have largely run their course, having ⁠lost much of their intimidating power”.
Speaking at an outdoor press conference as purple clouds lingered ominously in the background, Carney said: “Not for the first time, Vladimir Putin is lying about the situation on the ground. Sanctions are very real and they’re going to continue to increase as long as this war goes on.”
Carney had previously said he would not boycott a group photo with Putin out of respect for hosts China . But he said if he were to find himself next to the Russian president, he would make Canada’s position clear.
Carney met China’s president Xi Jinping on Tuesday, with the two countries announcing remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.
The two men also discussed AI, Carney said Wednesday, adding he had taken the opportunity to share Canada’s views on a model for global governance.
“The absence of any global governance around AI is an enormous risk,” he said. “It’s an enormous economic risk but it’s a biohazard risk, and it’s a risk to democracy, human dignity, other factors... So it is past time to develop global governance frameworks for these sectors.”
Carney is due to meet Donald Trump later today, he said, where they would discuss efforts to reach a trade deal.
“We have been making progress... Two steps forward, one step back type thing,” he said.
He said he fully respected Trump’s engagement with China.
“I’m going to say something positive here about the initiative around denuclearization, the trilateral meeting that is going to happen,” he said. “Guess what? Canada’s in favor of denuclearization. If the relationship can be used towards that end, we’re very much supportive of it.”
Donald Trump has arrived in Shenzhen, China, for the Apec summit, Chinese state media reported.
We will bring you more as we get it.
The Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, has arrived in China for the Apec summit , Reuters reports, in her first official visit to the country since becoming the leader of Japan.
Like Trump, she also travelled from Manila, the Philippines, where she met with the leaders of the US, Australia and India as part of the Quad (a security grouping of the four countries) held in parallel with the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean).
As Trump makes his way to China , he has posted a message on his Truth Social platform reflecting on his visit to the Philippines and his meeting with president Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

It was an Honor to be with him, and his beautiful wife and son.”

articles.title_orig: Nvidia says no longer shipping 'Hopper' AI chips to China
articles.title_zh: Nvidia says no longer shipping 'Hopper' AI chips to China
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.
The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.
It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.
Separately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.
Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump 's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.
CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.
On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang 's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.
Bessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.
In an August securities filing , Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.
Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

articles.title_orig: China’s Xi pitches free trade at APEC amid Trump’s global trade disruptions
articles.title_zh: China’s Xi pitches free trade at APEC amid Trump’s global trade disruptions
articles.content_orig:
China’s President Xi Jinping has urged support for “free and open trade”, pitching Beijing as a stable partner – as opposed to President Donald Trump-led Washington – and pledging to stand up to trade protectionism.
Speaking on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit on Wednesday in Shenzhen, southern China, Xi took aim at rising “unilateralism and protectionism”.
His remarks appeared to be a veiled criticism of Trump’s America First policies, under which the United States has imposed tariffs on both allies and economic rivals.
Xi is due to meet Trump, who is travelling from the Philippines for the APEC leaders’ summit later on Wednesday. Xi and Trump are then due to hold an unprecedented three-way summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
On the sidelines of the APEC summit, Xi told business executives that the Asia Pacific must pursue more open trade and equitable growth to remain stable and dynamic.
Trump’s America First approach of tariff hikes and other moves runs counter to APEC’s aim of eventually forming a Pacific Rim free trade zone.
Washington also limits Chinese access to leading-edge US technology, such as the Nvidia computer chips that help power artificial intelligence (AI).
“We must firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organization at its core, support free and open trade and investment, maintain the stability and smooth operation of global industrial and supply chains,” Xi said.
He added that China sought to “provide a more stable, predictable and beneficial environment for global enterprises” and would continue to expand access in its manufacturing and services sectors.
“Starting by lowering tariffs, expanding access, and exploring regulations and management standards, China will conduct deep-seated reform,” Xi said.
“While pursuing its own development, China has shared opportunities with other countries and worked for common development,” he said. “It has steadily brought stability and predictability to world economic growth and international trade and economic cooperation.”
George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, told the Associated Press news agency that Xi’s speech highlighted China’s aim to lead global industrial transformation.
“While he didn’t say so explicitly, his message was clear: China wants to be seen as a partner in global technology development, in contrast to Washington’s more restrictive approach,” Chen said, noting that Xi did not mention export controls, Nvidia, or the US directly.
Xi’s message is “likely to resonate with many Global South countries, and reinforces Beijing’s effort to contrast its technology strategy with that of Washington”, Chen added.

articles.title_orig: FAA oversaw and signed off on repair work before nationwide ground stop
articles.title_zh: FAA oversaw and signed off on repair work before nationwide ground stop
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration’s request for $50.1 billion in new Federal Aviation Administration funding after a nationwide ground stop strangled air travel is running into skepticism from both parties on Capitol Hill.
The funding request was suddenly increased from $30 billion after the hourslong ground stop Friday caused delays and cancellations for passengers across thousands of flights.
The formal funding ask was conveyed in a Tuesday letter signed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who refused to apologize or accept responsibility for the failure, blaming it on predecessors and Congress. The letter, cosigned by FAA chief Bryan Bedford and White House budget director Russell Vought, stated the money was needed “to deliver a truly world-class air traffic control network.”
After publicly reproaching Congress for the failure last week, Duffy met privately with Senate Republicans on Tuesday to make his case on Capitol Hill.
The closed-door briefing was contentious. The transportation secretary was “yelled at” by multiple Republican senators during his briefing, according to a person in the room who was not authorized to speak publicly about the private discussion.
When it was over, Senate Republican leaders and Duffy notably held their news conferences separately.
Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., stopped short of endorsing the full funding figure, saying only that the GOP is unified around the belief that “safe skies is an incredibly important priority.”
“We will see what the traffic will bear, what’s achievable,” he said, calling it a “discussion to be had” on the dollar amount.
Duffy met with only Republicans on Tuesday, not Democrats — even though the regular government funding process requires bipartisan support.
And Democrats were left wanting a better explanation, particularly as Duffy has pointed fingers at them. And members in both parties noted that President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” included $12.5 billion for air traffic control that still has not been fully used up.
“Look, we have not been given the answers. They have not come clean,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told reporters on Tuesday. “At his first press conference, all Duffy did was attack Democrats, and he asked for $50 billion when they haven’t even spent the $12 billion we’ve given to them. I have little faith in them.”
Facing Republican questions on the matter, Duffy insisted that the $12.5 billion was insufficient for the specific upgrades he deemed necessary in this situation.
Other Democrats are vexed by the FAA funding request.
“I generally support the idea of investing in air traffic control, but $50 billion sounds like an awfully round number,” said Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, who’s poised to become majority whip and also sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee.
The issue is wrapped up in a larger debate about funding the government ahead of a Dec. 11 deadline to avoid another shutdown . Congress could either reach a deal by then on new funding, punt it to next year with a stopgap bill, or fail to act and allow a shutdown.
Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, said air traffic control is “absolutely not a partisan issue” and that Congress will work to make sure that any funding is “paid for in a responsible way.”
Republicans are also considering a party-line “reconciliation” bill to approve military funding without the need for Democratic votes; Democrats are likely to resist additional military funds unless the Iran war comes to an end. Other provisions could be added to such a bill — if it materializes before Republicans lose control of Congress. Thune indicated Tuesday that it is still an open question, as Republicans would need to pass a budget resolution by Thanksgiving to pull it off. It would be a long, arduous process requiring near-total GOP unity in both chambers, and it would need to begin soon in order to finish this year.
Duffy said he’s agnostic on how the funds get passed when asked by NBC News why he only met with Republicans on Tuesday.
“I have met with Democrats. I’ve spent hours on the phone with Democrats. Get along with them well. They understand this issue,” Duffy said Tuesday, speaking to reporters separately after meeting with GOP senators. “I’m not going to tell them how to do their work, but I’m telling everybody what we need. I’m making a nice ask, and I’m going to let them work their process.”
One of the Democrats whom Duffy spoke to was House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely next House speaker.
“I appreciated the conversation,” Jeffries told reporters. “There are still more questions than answers in terms of what happened, why it happened, how do we prevent it from happening again.”
Jeffries added that he wants a briefing on the FAA ground stop and other recent outages, saying: “These developments are troubling, and it’s unclear if it’s all infrastructure-related or whether there’s some malignant activity.”
When asked about Duffy’s $50.1 billion request, outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said Republicans would work with the administration to fund “as much of that as we can.” He pointed to the $12.5 billion already approved for FAA modernization and did not specify a timeline or whether Congress would pursue a supplemental funding package.
I am a field producer for NBC News based in Washington, D.C., covering all things politics.
Sahil Kapur is a senior national political reporter for NBC News.
Julie Tsirkin is a correspondent covering Capitol Hill and the White House.

articles.title_orig: Leukemia vaccine passes key trial, adding to breakthrough year for cancer drugs
articles.title_zh: Leukemia vaccine passes key trial, adding to breakthrough year for cancer drugs
articles.content_orig:
For appointments, call: 800-525-2225
By Jim Stallard Tuesday, November 17, 2026
A cancer vaccine appears to significantly improve survival in people in remission from one of the most common and aggressive blood cancers, acute myeloid leukemia (AML) , according to new results from a phase 3 clinical trial.
The vaccine, galinpepimut-S (or GPS), was invented by David A. Scheinberg, MD, PhD , a leader in immunotherapy drug development at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK).
The clinical trial, which included 126 patients, was led by SELLAS Life Sciences Group. The study found:
As a therapeutic cancer vaccine, it works by teaching the immune system to fight remaining traces of cancer cells that may be undetectable following treatment, but ultimately can lead to a relapse.
The GPS is a complex “peptide” vaccine that triggers a targeted immune response by using synthetic peptides, which are the building blocks of proteins. The vaccine targets a protein called WT1, found in the cancer cells of more than 95% of people with AML (as well as in ovarian cancer, mesothelioma, and other cancers and leukemias).
The GPS vaccine is ready-made and “off-the-shelf” — as opposed to a personalized vaccine individually designed for each patient. Because off-the-shelf vaccines don’t need to be custom-manufactured, the hope is that they can be mass-produced, stored, and administered right away.
“Two decades of research have given us a much clearer picture of how the immune system can recognize and attack tumors and leukemias,” Dr. Scheinberg says. “These insights are helping lay the groundwork for these exciting, new immune-based approaches that could safely benefit more people with cancer. These data bring us closer to having the first off-the-shelf vaccine for AML patients.”
Although rare overall, acute myeloid leukemia is one of the most common types of blood cancer.  It moves quickly and needs aggressive, often harsh, treatment with chemotherapy , sometimes followed by a bone marrow transplant . Even when these therapies stop the cancer, AML often returns, and treatment options have been limited.
The trial’s results point to the potential of GPS as a completely new form of “maintenance immunotherapy,” which prevents the disease from returning after primary treatment. Dr. Scheinberg and his colleagues at MSK have been developing this peptide vaccine for more than two decades.
Dr. Scheinberg holds the Vincent Astor Chair .
Disclosure: Memorial Sloan Kettering (MSK) and Dr. Scheinberg have financial interests related to SELLAS Life Sciences.

articles.title_orig: South Korea’s high-stakes university exams upended by AI cheating scandal
articles.title_zh: South Korea’s high-stakes university exams upended by AI cheating scandal
articles.content_orig:
South Korea has been gripped by revelations of AI-aided cheating, just days before more than half a million students are to sit high-stakes entrance exams
The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.
On Thursday, more than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the exam, known as the suneung, at 1,312 centres across the country. The exam runs for a gruelling eight hours over a single day and determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.
The country goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended.
The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre. Extra trains run from 6am, police drive latecomers to their exam halls, and tourist attractions open late to ease traffic. Offices are asked to open at 10am.
But in recent days, exam organisers have faced a renewed threat to the validity of the entire exercise, after the top scorer in this year’s tax accountancy exam- who got just one question wrong out of 160– admitted on Sunday he had cheated by using AI.
Prime minister Han Seong-sook told a cabinet meeting in Seoul on Tuesday that AI-assisted cheating was a “social evil” that the government would “root out”.
“We will block outright the carrying of smart devices during the exam,” she said. The education ministry and other agencies should approach it “as if staking their jobs on it”, she added.
Han said smart devices must be turned off and handed in, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.
The government will also send emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sound at full volume and cannot be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.
More invigilators will be deployed, and the government said it was preparing to switch off school wifi inside exam centres and public wifi nearby, and that personal hotspots, which cannot be blocked, would be traced through connection records.
The weekend’s cheating revelation captured national headlines in South Korea , stoking concern about the security of the suneung.
In a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the exam cheat said he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”
His lawyer handed police a camera, a laptop and a phone. No charges have been brought, and the prime minister has ordered procedures to begin that would void his result and bar him for five years.
The education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, told parliament on Monday that while authorities could screen out the smart glasses already on sale at Thursday’s exam, newer variants could not be dealt with perfectly.
Choi has ruled out postponing the exam , which has been delayed several times before, including in 2017 , after an earthquake struck the south-eastern city of Pohang, and in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic.
Smart glasses have been banned in exams since the end of June. In October, several candidates were caught with them while sitting university-run admissions exams. At the suneung, wearing a pair counts as using one even when switched off.
The education ministry looked at using radio-frequency equipment to detect the glasses in exam halls, but concluded conditions varied too much between venues for deployment this year. Checks will instead rely on visual inspection, with at least one dedicated official placed in each exam centre.
Teachers’ unions have criticised the government response as belated. A survey last month of 2,716 secondary school teachers by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union showed that 82.3% said they could not tell whether a candidate was wearing smart glasses under the current procedure, with only 3.5% saying they could.
To avoid facing scrutiny on exam day, some candidates are reportedly switching to contact lenses. An optician in Suwon, south of Seoul, said students who had never worn contacts were coming in to ask how to put them in.
Han said on X on Monday that the checks would be handled carefully “so that candidates acting in good faith do not suffer unnecessary anxiety or inconvenience”.
In his video confession, the accountancy test cheat addressed suneung candidates directly. “The suneung is coming up soon,” he said.
“To anyone thinking of cheating as I did: I am going to tell the investigators everything, so please don’t think, ‘I won’t get caught.’”

articles.title_orig: Modi Tries to End Photo-Op With Trump in Awkward Quad Briefing
articles.title_zh: Modi Tries to End Photo-Op With Trump in Awkward Quad Briefing
articles.content_orig:
Leaders of India and Japan join for talks on military exercises, AI and rare earths as a counter to Chinese power
Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese have heralded plans for new joint Quad military exercises designed to push back on China’s expansionist ambitions, with the US president promising the grouping with India and Japan will guarantee “peace through strength”.
Albanese met Trump, India’s Nahrendra Modi and Japan’s Sanae Takaichi in Manila late on Tuesday in talks about enhanced cooperation on AI, critical minerals, infrastructure and maritime security.
“These nations represent some of the most important partnerships in the entire world,” the US president said.
“They’re among the most successful nations in the world, and in certain ways among the most powerful nations of the world. Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific.”
Trump said: “As we continue to protect peace through strength, we are also working together to advance super intelligence, SI, the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the industrial revolution.”
The Australian prime minister praised Trump and said a new Quad business forum to be held in 2027 would build economic growth across the region.
Leaders in the group – established as China seeks to build its military might and exert influence across the region – say they will cooperate to maintain peace and stability with Beijing.
“When we work together for our common view in the Indo-Pacific of peace, security, stability, and prosperity, then the world will be a safer and more secure place, and the Quad has a critical role in achieving that,” Albanese told the summit.
The plan for new military exercises involving maritime patrol aircraft is likely to prompt strong criticism from China.
Albanese said Australia would deploy its P8-A Poseidon and P3-C Orion maritime patrol aircraft as part of the operation in early 2027.
Asked what he would tell Chinese leader Xi Jinping later this week about the plan, Albanese said military exercises were common.
“We want peace and security in the region. That’s the objective here. It’s not about any one country. It’s about our own sovereignty, but also about peace and security in the region,” he said
The Quad leaders want the group to present a multilateral coalition of resistance against Beijing, seeking to undermine its dominance, including in the South and East China seas .
Takaichi said the Quad would help shape the future of the region.
“We would like to realise a free and open Indo Pacific by strengthening resilience of countries in the region and promote their freedom to decide for themselves across a wide range of areas including maritime security, economic security, energy and critical and emerging technologies.”
Before the meeting, as the four leaders posed for a group photo, Trump praised Modi and Takaichi as “tough”, before gesturing to Albanese and saying: “We’re OK too.” Albanese laughed at the remark.
The first meeting of the Quad leaders since 2024 came as Albanese and Trump both prepare for setpiece engagement with China’s president later this week. Albanese will visit Xi in Shenzhen on Friday, a day after three-way talks between Trump, Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Trump said he wanted talks with the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, but conceded he was not the host of the China summit and it was up to Xi to issue an invitation. The US president said he could have a one-on-one meeting with Putin “if it’s available”.
Quad military exercises would build on progress from the recently completed Malabar joint exercise near Japan , where sailors completed anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare drills.
Trump also talked up the Aukus nuclear deal with Australia. “We make the greatest submarines anywhere in the world, and we’re working with Australia and others on that,” he said.
Trump said the US was poised to catch up to China on rare earth production within 10 months, backed up by speedy progress from Australia, Japan and India .
He was accompanied by cabinet members Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent, Howard Lutnick and Jamieson Greer, as well as his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller.
Privately, officials believed the meeting alone showed the group was progressing. Australian officials welcomed the engagement of Trump in regional affairs as he enters the final two years of his presidency.
Trump took credit for reinvigorating the grouping, and said he placed a premium on relations with Albanese, Modi and Takaichi.
“When they have difficulty, when they want to tell me something, my phone is always open, and the Oval Office is always open to you, and you know that,” he said.
Albanese said before the meeting he would push Trump on ending the war in Iran, a conflict which has produced an unprecedented global energy shock and badly distorted conditions in the Australian economy.
It was Albanese’s first meeting with Takaichi since a weeks-long saga about comments he made on a podcast about her gift of melons presented to him during a visit to Australia in July.
Earlier, Albanese took part in the East Asia Summit where he called for regional partners to work together to boost AI protections. Trump, who calls the technology “superintelligence” , said it represented “the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution”.

articles.title_zh: Framework Launches Customizable Slim Wireless Touchpad Keyboard With Open-Source CAD Files
articles.content_orig:
Logitech’s K400 may have met its match.﻿
Logitech’s K400 may have met its match.﻿
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Framework announced its Wireless Touchpad Keyboard earlier this year with the goal of delivering a better couch keyboarding experience than the Logitech K400 . According to The Verge ’s Sean Hollister who went hands-on with Framework’s new all-in-one keyboard and touchpad last April, the company has succeeded in that goal, but it turns out you’ll be paying a bit more for Framework’s than Logitech’s.
While the K400 couch keyboard is $35, the Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard is $99 with a $50 fully refundable deposit required to preorder one starting today . That makes it nearly three times more expensive than Logitech’s, but Framework’s upgrades and improvements could make it worth the premium.
Instead of starting from scratch, Framework uses the same keyboard module found in its Laptop 12 paired with a precision 120Hz touchpad and controller that’s also used in all of the company’s computers. A Bluetooth connection is the easiest way to pair the keyboard to PCs running Windows, Linux, or macOS, or mobile devices, game consoles, and streaming boxes. You can quickly switch between four wirelessly connected devices with a button press including one that uses an included USB receiver. If you want more responsiveness, you can also tether it to a device with a USB-C cable.
On a full charge of its replaceable 1,200mAh battery the keyboard will run for well over a year with sporadic use. If you’re instead using it for hours every day on a desk, Framework estimates the battery life will be closer to over a month. For customizability and remapping the keyboard’s open source firmware is based on a fork of ZMK .

articles.title_orig: Xi calls for greater Asia-Pacific trade openness ahead of Trump’s China visit (FXI:NYSEARCA)
articles.title_zh: Xi calls for greater Asia-Pacific trade openness ahead of Trump’s China visit (FXI:NYSEARCA)
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — Chinese President Xi Jinping opened a key Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting on Wednesday with calls for removing trade and investment barriers.
The leader spoke as he was expected to host Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump this week alongside the APEC CEO and Economic Leaders Summit.
"We should remove trade and investment barriers," Xi said via an official English translation. He said a key reason for doing so was "to promote development that is balanced."
He did not mention U.S. tariffs or other specific measures. Instead, Xi cast China as a "promising land for development" for global businesses, and indicated plans for "Bay Area" cooperation.
Shenzhen, home to major Chinese tech companies, is part of China's "Greater Bay Area" that includes Hong Kong and Macau. The Silicon Valley region around San Francisco is also known as the "Bay Area" in the U.S.
"China will not only cut tariffs and expand market access, but also go a step further," Xi said. He said China would "reform" rules and regulations to give foreign businesses "full manufacturing access."
Chinese exports have steadily grown their share of global manufactured goods, drawing criticism from the European Union and other regions for overcapacity. The U.S. and China last year agreed to keep tariffs lower, but the world's two largest economies have yet to implement a planned $30 billion cut in duties on goods from each side.
"Global growth lacks momentum," Xi noted in his speech. But he said "still global trade keeps growing against headwinds, and breakthroughs are being made in emerging technologies at a faster pace."
He said the "hard questions of our times" for Asia Pacific economies is whether to open, or close, doors — and later cast opening doors as bringing "progress."
"There can be no stability without security, and no security without stability," he said.
Xi called for APEC members to deepen coordination in the digital economy and AI, as a way to drive regional economic growth.
"Unicorn companies and large AI models have emerged in large numbers and many innovations have empowered hundreds of trades and industries and reached millions of households," he said, in some of his most specific mentions of the cutting-edge technology.

articles.title_zh: Trump Lauds Defense Alliance With Philippines Ahead of China Talks
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
GUANGZHOU, China — Behind the scenes, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spent months pushing for action that would signal resolve within the Trump administration against China’s pursuit of the most powerful American computer chips, a flashpoint  in their race for superiority in artificial intelligence, multiple sources said.
But President Trump’s courtship of Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, seeking to alleviate tensions between the world’s greatest powers, and a contingent of advisors skeptical of commercial warfare against Beijing slowed the process down — giving China months of opportunity to gain access to U.S. semiconductors through the back door.
Ultimately, just hours before departing for Asia alongside  Trump, Bessent got his way, bolstering his position ahead of talks with Chinese officials in Shenzhen this week on the risks posed by frontier systems.
A new rule tightening loopholes in U.S. export controls sends a dual message to Beijing ahead of Thursday’s summit: that Washington is serious about curbing Chinese circumvention — and that China hawks within the administration may be gaining the upper hand.
Trump has repeatedly sidestepped confrontation with Xi over the intensifying AI race in their two previous meetings this year, in Beijing and Washington, wary of upsetting a carefully managed detente and reluctant to jeopardize a technology boom increasingly central to the U.S. economy.
The new rules restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best AI models.
But the administration, from the president down, is acutely aware of China’s ambitions to dominate an industry that could reshape the global balance of power. That competitive drive was underscored this month by a scandal involving a Chinese espionage campaign targeting Jensen Huang, co-founder of Nvidia, the world’s leading AI chip maker.
Before resigning from the company in disgrace Thursday, Huang admitted to having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy — a woman who worked at a firm in Singapore accused by American authorities of helping to divert restricted Nvidia chips to China, in violation of U.S. export controls.
The national security scandal has roiled the markets — and in so doing, commanded Trump’s attention — inflicting a significant devaluation on Nvidia and reverberating well beyond it, wiping nearly $1 trillion from the combined market value of major technology companies in a single trading session on Monday.
Trump, who counts Huang a friend and ally, indicated he would be open to his return as Nvidia’s chief executive. Bessent suggested otherwise, expressing confidence its board could find competent new leadership and urging a full investigation.
Huang indicated his interest Tuesday in returning to Nvidia, writing in a social media post that “I would be honored” to resume his role as CEO if asked by the board of directors. But Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said later Tuesday that the company does not intend to bring Huang back.
Trump is not expected to raise the Nvidia matter directly with Xi. But Bessent plans to do so in his own meetings, one official said.
The Treasury secretary has thus taken on the role of an enforcer, pursuing a tougher line than Trump is willing to take himself in his highly personalized relationship with the Chinese leader.
Bessent is scheduled to meet with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on the sidelines of the summitry in Shenzhen to discuss potential collaboration on AI safety protocols, standards for testing of advanced models, and a direct communications channel for AI emergencies.
The two men have met before to discuss AI, most recently in New York, where they agreed in principle to coordinate. But the talks have yet to produce much in the way of tangible results.
“Bessent is signaling that, while he sees working with Beijing to mitigate AI risks as a priority, it won’t come at the expense of actions that he sees as necessary to protect U.S. national security, like limiting AI chip exports to China,” said Daniel Remler, a senior fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a New American Security.
The administration’s latest action marks a policy defeat for Howard Lutnick , secretary of the Commerce Department, who oversees chip policy and had advocated for a less restrictive approach than Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative.
The feud began spilling into public view ahead of the president’s travel, and in light of the Nvidia scandal, after Bessent said in a television interview that the Commerce Department “has the pen” to act, implying a split within the team.
“Look, there’re two different views,” Trump told reporters Monday, answering questions on the matter. “One view is you don’t want to insult China. We have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them.”
“The other view is just go, you know, down and dirty and do what you have to do,” Trump continued. “You can’t say either is wrong or right. We’ll let you know.”
Beyond the diplomatic niceties, Trump has been explicit and consistent since resuming office that the United States must “win” the race for AI superiority, calling the alternative “not acceptable.”
“Whoever wins AI,” Trump said at the United Nations General Assembly in September, “whoever wins superintelligence, wins.”
Trump will arrive in China on Wednesday after meeting with world leaders in Manila, including those from the Quad — an alliance of Japan, India, Australia and the United States —  who discussed AI at their own summit Tuesday evening.
Describing “superintelligence” — Trump’s preferred term for AI — as “the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution,” Trump announced a Quad effort to accelerate adoption of the technology, including an investment of more than $85 million to enhance AI ecosystems throughout the region.
“We want to be careful with it,” Trump said, “but it’s amazing, the things that have come out, in terms of science and in terms of medical breakthroughs. No one can believe what we’re finding. And we’re finding it fast.”
“We want to be very careful, but we want to cherish it,” he added. “The United States as you know is leading in that capacity, by quite a bit.”
As he meets with the leaders of India, Japan and Australia, Trump will face pressure to sustain resolve against Beijing despite his yearlong courtship of President Xi Jinping.
The new U.S. rule requires overseas data centers serving customers in China, Russia, Iran and Cuba to identify their end users before gaining access to chips. It also imposes additional licensing requirements on chip sales to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which the Commerce Department identifies as posing a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to unauthorized destinations.
U.S. officials say that export controls are not up for negotiation in talks with the Chinese. But Beijing sees them as yet another historic example of Washington trying to contain its rise — a posture that has repeatedly stifled diplomatic progress between the two superpowers.
“While administration officials say export controls aren’t up for negotiation, Chinese officials will certainly bring them up,” Remler said. “These restrictions are the key obstacle to China’s AI progress, which is increasingly important to the Chinese economy and to Xi’s strategic goals.”
China claims it does not seek an all-powerful, generalized “superintelligence,” but rather specialized AI systems embedded across industries to boost productivity and improve quality of life.

articles.title_orig: Morning Bid: Jensen Huang's last hurrah, and a nervy future for Nvidia
articles.title_zh: Morning Bid: Jensen Huang's last hurrah, and a nervy future for Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.
Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.
Kress has served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013. During her tenure, she has led the company’s finance organization and has played a key role in NVIDIA’s growth and evolution. Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.
The Board of Directors appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever Chair of the Board.  Mr. Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys.
“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, Chair of the NVIDIA Board of Directors. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”
“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Colette Kress, Interim CEO and CFO, NVIDIA. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”
Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.
NVIDIA will report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results on Tuesday, November 17, at approximately 1:20 p.m. PT, as previously scheduled, followed by its earnings call at 2 p.m. PT.

articles.title_orig: Colette Kress Just Delivered Excellent News for Nvidia Investors
articles.title_zh: Colette Kress Just Delivered Excellent News for Nvidia Investors
articles.content_orig:
AI investors and beyond were eagerly anticipating Nvidia's ( NVDA -0.44% ) earnings call Tuesday night. The earnings report was the company's first since Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO amid controversy last week. Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress as the interim CEO as it conducts a search for a permanent replacement, considering both internal and external candidates.
Kress passed her first test with flying colors, as she delivered a confident pitch for the company and even raised guidance for fiscal 2028 from 70% revenue growth to 75% revenue growth. Nvidia also beat estimates on the top and bottom lines, and the stock was trading higher after the call, up 3.3% as of 8:23 p.m.
However, amid the focus on the headline numbers and parsing the call for hints into the company's future, there was one key comment from Kress that investors may have missed.
It's understandable why Nvidia is down a third from its peak last month, given Huang's sudden exit, but with Nvidia stock now trading at a forward P/E of just 11, the stock is as cheap as it's ever been and ripe for share buybacks.
In response to a question about the company's capital allocation and its buyback plans, Kress said that the "super top priority" for returning capital to shareholders was to use the company's current share repurchase authorization, which was raised by $150 billion in September and sat at $227.3 billion at the end of the third quarter. Kress added, "So thinking about all of that together, I think there is definitely room to continue all of the stock repurchase plans that we want to do and complete those before the end of fiscal year '28." She also noted that the top priority for its capital spending is supporting its suppliers in building out additional capacity.
If Nvidia executes on those buybacks and the stock price stays roughly the same, it would reduce shares outstanding by roughly 6% by Jan. 2028, when fiscal 2028 ends.
The share repurchase authorization and Kress's commitment are a positive sign, not just because it will lift Nvidia's earnings per share, but because it shows management's confidence that the stock is undervalued after the recent sell-off and signals to investors that it's worth buying.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/17/26
For investors worried that Nvidia would struggle during the transitional period, Kress gave no indication that anything has changed, saying, "it's business as usual," and that customers, suppliers, and partners are all "100% behind us."
Demand for the company's products continues to outstrip supply, and Kress spent much of the call reiterating the company's commitment to securing adequate supply, which allowed it to raise its revenue guidance for fiscal 2028.
In just one quarter, its supply commitments increased from $279 billion, primarily due to memory supply. Kress said, "We feel confident in terms of both the demand that we have in front of us as well as the supply and additionally that we can do the 75%," referring to 75% revenue growth next year.
Nvidia also addressed the controversy around Jensen Huang, and new Chairman of the Board Harvey Jones made it clear that the board has no intention of reinstating Huang. Regarding the CEO search, Jones said, "We want to install this CEO, the permanent CEO, as quickly as possible, but we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person." Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, who has been seen as a possible replacement for Huang, was on the Q&A portion of the call, but did not answer any questions.
Nvidia did what it needed to do on the earnings call and then some. Its commitment to using up its $227 billion share repurchase authorization and the guidance hike for fiscal 2028 show investors the company continues to excel. Nvidia is on track to bring in more than $700 billion in revenue next year. Given the deep discount, Nvidia looks like a buy , even without Jensen Huang.

articles.title_orig: Stock futures rise as Nvidia gains on earnings beat and solid outlook: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures rise as Nvidia gains on earnings beat and solid outlook: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures climbed Wednesday morning after the S&P 500 fell for a fourth straight day. Traders also weighed Nvidia 's better-than-expected earnings report.
Nasdaq-100 futures were up 0.61%, while S&P 500 futures added 0.25%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures traded up 25 points, close to the flatline.
In Asia, markets were mixed in a choppy session, with Japan's Nikkei 225 up 0.45% after the country reported a sharp 20.5% jump in exports last month. South Korea's Kospi rose 1.85% as chip heavyweights soared on Nvidia's earnings beat. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was 1.05% lower, while mainland China's CSI 300 was flat. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 lost 0.69%.
Shares of Nvidia jumped 4% in extended trading after the company's profit and revenue in the third quarter beat analysts' estimates. The company also lifted its revenue guidance for the fiscal year ending January 2028, calling for 75% growth year over year.
"The fact that they gave guidance is huge," said Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, on CNBC's "Closing Bell: Overtime. " " That is a very bullish sign. I expect the stock to move higher based just on that alone."
Neocloud companies also rose in extended trading. CoreWeave advanced 8%, while Nebius Group gained 10%.
During the regular trading day, the Dow dropped 1.6%. The S&P 500 slipped 1% and notched its lowest closing level since July 29, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 0.7%. During the day, the tech-heavy index touched its lowest level since April.
Heading into Wednesday, traders are awaiting building permits and housing starts data. The Federal Open Market Committee's minutes from its October meeting will also be out in the afternoon. Federal Reserve policymakers last month decided to keep the overnight funds rate in a range of 3.75% to 4%.
On the earnings front, Lowe's, Target and TJ Maxx-parent TJX Cos are slated to report Wednesday morning.
Later this week, investors are awaiting a blockbuster initial public offering from Anthropic. The AI giant's shares are expected to be priced above the current range between $70 and $78, multiple sources told CNBC's David Faber on Tuesday.
Major Asian tech names gained Wednesday after chip giant Nvidia reported an earnings beat overnight in its first set of results without former CEO Jensen Huang.
Memory heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix rose 1.21% and 5.1%, respectively, while Japanese semiconductor equipment testers Advantest and Lasertec climbed 4.02% and 4.35%. Tech investor SoftBank Group rose 3.29%.
Taiwan's TSMC saw a smaller gain, trading just above the flatline.
West Texas Intermediate futures fell 1.06% to $85.13 per barrel on Wednesday.
Futures for the international benchmark Brent saw a smaller decline, down 0.35% at $92.81 per barrel.
The fall in prices comes even as Kuwait reported "hostile drone attacks," with hostilities in the Middle East region appearing to be on the boil again.
Japan's exports in October surged 20.5% from a year earlier, snapping a two-month slowdown in shipments, official data released Wednesday showed.
Exports growth beat expectations of economists polled by Reuters that had pegged it at 20%, and it was sharply higher compared to 16.5% in September.
Shipments of semiconductor equipment that have been propping up Tokyo's exports jumped 49.7% by value. Exports of motor vehicles climbed 19.9% year on year.
In terms of destinations, shipments to China rose 13.3%, while they climbed 23.9% to the U.S.
Asia markets opened higher Wednesday, with South Korea leading gains in the region as chip heavyweights soared on Nvidia's earnings beat.
The Kospi was  2.9% higher, with heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix climbing 4.47% and 5.83% respectively. Both companies are Nvidia suppliers.
Japan's Nikkei 225 was up 1.1% after the country reported a sharp 20.5% jump in exports last month, although the broad-based Topix was trading close to the flatline.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was down 0.39%.
Asian markets were set to open mixed on Wednesday, after Wall Street closed lower overnight.
Japan's Nikkei 225 is set for a stronger open, with futures in Chicago at 59,835 and in Osaka last at 58,890 compared to the index Tuesday close of 58,860. The country is set to report October trade data, with Reuters-poll estimates pegging exports growth at 20%.
Futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index were last at 23,414, lower than its close of 23,508.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 started the day 0.26% down.
Traders appeared to look past a report from The Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar, that the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating artificial intelligence bellwether Nvidia .
The Journal's report arrives on the heels of a rocky week for the chip giant, whose CEO Jensen Huang resigned after reports of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Shares of Nvidia were last up more than 4% on the back of a third-quarter earnings beat and a strong revenue growth outlook for the fiscal year ending in January 2028.
Stock futures rose on Tuesday after Nvidia reported better-than-expected earnings and strong guidance.
Nasdaq-100 futures were up 1.37% while S&P 500 futures added 0.82%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures climbed over 170 points or 0.34%.

articles.title_orig: Waymo suspends driverless freeway rides across US after California ban
articles.title_zh: Waymo suspends driverless freeway rides across US after California ban
articles.content_orig:
Waymo has paused its driverless taxi services on freeways across the United States after California temporarily banned the ride-hailing platform on the state’s highways over safety concerns.
A spokesperson for the California-based company – a subsidiary of Alphabet, Google’s parent company – said it has “temporarily restricted commercial freeway rides in all markets where we operate that service”, but it is “continuing freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel”.
Waymo implemented the suspension last Wednesday, according to the spokesperson, but they did not say how long it would last.
Along with California, the driverless vehicles will pause highway services in Phoenix, Austin and Miami. Waymo offers rides on city streets in areas including Las Vegas, Dallas and Denver.
The spokesperson said the suspension would allow the company to “evaluate our performance” following incidents in California and that it prioritises safety.
One incident on November 6 went viral after video captured on a San Francisco highway showed a Waymo vehicle speeding towards and attempting to pass two police cars, even as their lights were flashing in an intentional bid to slow traffic.
The officers were driving behind a slow-moving construction truck.
The episode led the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) to temporarily ban Waymo vehicles from its highways, effective from November 11.
The DMV, which is responsible for road safety, said its decision was also prompted by a November 5 incident, when three Waymo autonomous vehicles drove into a construction zone in the San Francisco Bay Area.
Waymo said the construction zone incident did not result in injuries or collisions.
DMV spokesman Jonathan Groveman said in a statement that “similar incidents” occurred on May 18.
“The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” he said.
The restrictions “will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates … it has taken effective corrective actions”, the statement read.
Waymo completes half a million trips each week and says it has demonstrated a 95 percent reduction in serious crashes as compared with human-driven vehicles.
It has been testing its vehicles in London since 2016, and has plans to expand into Munich and Madrid in 2027.

articles.title_orig: Target is set to report earnings before the bell. Here's what to expect
articles.title_zh: Target is set to report earnings before the bell. Here's what to expect
articles.content_orig:
Target is expected to report fiscal third-quarter results on Wednesday and offer more details on the progress of its turnaround as the company prepares for the busy holiday season.
The big-box retailer has been showing signs of returning to growth, as it sees stronger sales trends after years of flat revenue. Last quarter, Target hiked its full fiscal-year outlook and said it saw "broad-based" strength across its various categories.
It's also lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in an effort to get customers back into its stores, especially as consumer sentiment lags and inflation remains high.
Here's what Wall Street is expecting for the retailer's fiscal third quarter, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
Despite the progress, CEO Michael Fiddelke has emphasized that the company remains cautious about its turnaround, saying after Target's second-quarter results that the retailer has "much more work to do." While categories like food and beauty saw encouraging sales trends, the apparel and home categories lagged during that quarter.
Some investors still aren't sure Target has done enough to show a steady turnaround. Analysts at Morgan Stanley wrote in a note last week that they expect Target to deliver an "encouraging" quarter, though questions about the broader health of the business remain.
"Target has an opportunity to demonstrate progress, but the durability and profitability of its recovery remain open questions," the analysts wrote.
Still, they said they believe the company's investments in the store experience are driving interest from consumers.
Target's stock is up more than 60% this year.

articles.title_orig: Iran Attacks Kuwait and Bahrain, Further Escalating Fight Over Strait
articles.title_zh: Iran Attacks Kuwait and Bahrain, Further Escalating Fight Over Strait
articles.content_orig:
Bahrain and Kuwait claimed Wednesday that they repelled air attacks launched against them, as Gulf nations face retaliatory bombardment following U.S. strikes on an Iranian island.The Iranian army said Wednesday its drones "targeted Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms belonging to the terrorist U.S. military at Ali Al-Salem Air Base in Kuwait," in a statement carried by state television IRIB.
Kuwait's military said Wednesday its air defenses were "responding to hostile drone threats" and urged the public to follow security and safety advice.
The foreign ministry said in a statement posted on social media that "the continuation of these attacks constitutes a dangerous escalation that threatens the region's security and stability and undermines diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalation."
Meanwhile, Bahrain said its air defenses intercepted attacks early Wednesday, a day after Tehran's Revolutionary Guard said it struck a base used by  the U.S.
Iran's official IRNA news agency cited a regional official as saying the United States had hit Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz  but did not cause serious damage.
Iraq has resumed pumping oil to Turkey through a pipeline at an initial capacity of 120,000 barrels a day, Oil Minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair al-Abadi said Tuesday in comments carried by state media. The export capacity will be gradually increased to reach 500,000 barrels a day, he said.
The capacity is fairly small compared to other pipelines in the region. The Saudi East-West pipeline, which crosses from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea in order to avoid the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Strait, has a capacity of 7 million barrels per day.
In August, Iraq and Turkey signed a deal to increase oil exports through a pipeline to the Turkish Mediterranean port of Ceyhan.
Iraq is moving to strengthen the resilience of its oil export infrastructure following the U.S.-Iran war's disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Iraq-Turkey pipeline has been largely idle since 2023 following legal and commercial disputes.
The United Arab Emirates' oil firm ADNOC said Wednesday that a crew member was missing after one of its ships was struck the night before in the Strait of Hormuz.
"All other crew members have been safely evacuated from the vessel. Eleven sustained injuries and where required are receiving medical care," ADNOC said, adding that search and rescue operations were continuing.
Monitoring agencies report ships being attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz on a near-daily basis. Iran claims it carried out some of the attacks on ships it considers transiting through the waterway without its permission.
The U.S. military has also previously said it struck and halted ships it deems to be violating its naval blockade on Iranian ports.
The U.S. launched precision strikes on an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps missile site on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to a U.S. military official.
The official said the strike was launched "in self-defense."
"The strike was in response to IRGC aggression targeting U.S. personnel and assets," the official said. "U.S. Central Command remains highly vigilant and fully postured to protect Americans across the region."
While the official did not specifically mention the IRGC aggression, the strikes came hours after Iran targeted a U.S. radar site in Bahrain. The s
This was the third attempted strike by Iran on a U.S. military installation in the last five days. All of them were intercepted, U.S. officials said.trikes were successfully intercepted, according to U.S. Central Command.
Iran had earlier said the U.S. attacked Qeshm Island, but they "caused no damage to residential, commercial, or infrastructural areas," according to Ahmad Nafisi, deputy provincial governor of the southern province of Hormozgan, quoted by the official IRNA news agency.
