articles.title_orig: Java4Shell Flaw (CVE-2026-114938) Enables Pre-Auth RCE in Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak and More
articles.title_zh: Java4Shell Flaw (CVE-2026-114938) Enables Pre-Auth RCE in Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak and More
articles.content_orig:
A Java flaw called Java4Shell can let attackers without an account run their own code on Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak, and three other widely used applications, says Calif, the security research firm that disclosed it this week.
The flaw is present in Java 17.0.6 and later, and the vulnerable code runs only on x86-64 Intel and AMD chips that support the AVX-512 VBMI feature.
Tracked as CVE-2026-114938 , the fix was released today by Oracle and the OpenJDK project, whose open-source code underpins Java builds from many vendors. Amazon has fixed its Corretto Java builds, but Red Hat is still preparing fixes for its own.
The researchers are holding back their attack code for the six applications, and other labs have so far reproduced crashes and a memory leak but not the code execution. Canada's Cyber Center said this week that it was not aware of any attacks exploiting the flaw.
Servers often decode Base64-encoded data, such as HTTP Basic login headers, SAML artifacts, and CSRF tokens, before checking whether a user is logged in. That is how an attacker without an account can exploit the flaw.
The flaw is in a faster version of Java's Base64 decoder that runs on chips with AVX-512 VBMI. Java switches to it after compiling the decoder for speed, which it does for code that runs often.
A malformed string that ends with an extra = makes this decoder write 62 or 63 bytes past the end of its output. Java rejects the string, but only after the write.
The bytes written past the end are fixed, so an attacker controls only where they land. For that reason, early readings of the source code had pointed to a crash rather than code execution, as The Hacker News noted in an earlier report yesterday.
The attacks worked without a login under the default settings of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, Calif says in its technical write-up . The researchers' lists are incomplete, and they rate the flaw as 9.2 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0.
They get past the fixed bytes by arranging the server's memory so that the overflow expands a neighboring array. They then use that array to write bytes of their choosing and a second array to read back from memory, a step they call JavaBleed. From there, the researchers say, the attack reaches the parts of Java that run code.
There is no single exploit that works everywhere. Each target requires its own memory layout and timing, and some attacks are sensitive to network delays.
A proxy that waits for complete requests, as nginx does by default, blocks some attacks but not all. A failed attempt can crash Java, and an attacker can often try again.
Security company Upwind reproduced the memory corruption on an AWS server with an Intel Ice Lake chip, where it damaged the next object in memory and eventually crashed Java, according to its lab results .
Blackpoint Cyber's Adversary Pursuit Group crashed a test Spring Boot application by sending about 28,300 malformed login requests over roughly 20 seconds, without ever logging in.
The group also used the JavaBleed step in a local test to read a secret stored next to the overflow, which worked in all 30 runs. It did not reproduce remote code execution, its test results show.
Oracle scores the flaw 8.1 out of 10 under CVSS 3.1, rating it hard to exploit but requiring no login. The description in its CVE record says, "Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE."
Red Hat also rates it as requiring no login, with a preliminary score of 9.8 out of 10. Amazon scores it 8.8 out of 10 and describes the risk in its Amazon Linux entry as "a JVM crash for unauthenticated users or, in certain application environments, code execution by an authenticated low-privileged user."
Canada's Cyber Centre also describes the flaw as exploitable remotely without authentication in its government alert .
The flaw was not in the KEV catalog of exploited vulnerabilities, kept by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), when The Hacker News checked it today.
The vulnerable code is in Java 17.0.6 and later on the Java 17 line, and in Java 21, 25, and 27. Standard Java 8 and Java 11 do not contain it, but the Java SE 8 Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf is affected. GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21.0.3, GraalVM for JDK 21.0.13.0.3, and GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20.0.3 are also affected.
It runs only on x86-64 chips that support AVX-512 VBMI. These include Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, and Granite Rapids chips, as well as AMD Zen 4 or newer chips. ARM64 chips do not run it.
Because the vulnerable code runs only on these chips, the same container image can run it on one server and not on another. On Linux, this command shows whether a server's chip has the four features the vulnerable code needs, and all four must appear in its output:
grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'
The attacker also needs malformed Base64 to reach Java's standard decoder, through paths such as the login headers and tokens described earlier.
Calif also says a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if the program runs no service of its own. The exploit for this came from another researcher, samczsun, and the researchers have not published how it reaches the decoder.
The OpenJDK project's vulnerability advisory lists the flaw as fixed in this week's releases, and Oracle's security advisory lists the affected versions of its builds.
For Oracle Java, the fixed builds are the new .1 releases in the table, all released this week. The release notes for 17.0.21.1 say it includes the update's security fixes, and the notes for 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1 say the same.
For the Java 8 Performance Pack, the latest build is 8u513, available in both standard and Performance Pack versions. For GraalVM, the November security releases are GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21.1, GraalVM for JDK 21.0.13.1, and GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20.1.
The Corretto changelog for 17.0.21.1.2 lists the flaw as fixed, as do the changelogs for the new 21, 25, and 27 builds. Amazon Linux also marks its Corretto 17, 21, 25 and 27 packages as fixed.
Azul's November update fixes the flaw in Zulu 17, 21, 25 and 27, according to its Zulu release notes .
Red Hat has not yet released fixes for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9 and 10, or for its OpenJDK 17, 21 and 25 builds, according to its security bulletin . Containers based on its images need to be rebuilt once updated images are out.
SAP released SapMachine 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, and 27.0.1.1 this week, but their release pages do not specify what they fix. Eclipse Temurin, the Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, and BellSoft Liberica had not listed fixed builds when The Hacker News checked today.
Products that bundle their own Java runtime need an update from the product's maker. After updating, restart Java services, and rebuild and redeploy container images so the running process uses the new build.
If you cannot update yet, start the JVM with one of these flags, and remove it once the fixed build is installed:
In Upwind's lab, both flags stopped the overflow on every affected version it tested. The company warns that another flag, -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock, stops Java from starting when it is used on its own.
To spot attempts, it suggests checking for the signs below, while warning that none of them proves a compromise and that their absence does not prove a server is safe:
A malformed input that triggers the overflow was posted publicly on September 9, in a proposed fix submitted to OpenJDK's code repository as a pull request . The proposal described an overflow in the same AVX-512 Base64 decoder code.
Its author closed it without merging it in early November, after an automated notice that it ha

articles.title_orig: China's Xi calls for upholding postwar international order at APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen
articles.title_zh: China's Xi calls for upholding postwar international order at APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen
articles.content_orig:
Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy
I n a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping , is basking in its neon glow.
On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.
The broader Apec summit , meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.
All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.
“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”
Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.
Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.
Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.
A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.
The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.
“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”
China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”
The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.
The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”
For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”
For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

articles.title_orig: Putin says EU is losing industry, falling behind competition ahead of meeting with Trump, Xi
articles.title_zh: Putin says EU is losing industry, falling behind competition ahead of meeting with Trump, Xi
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — Russian President Vladimir Putin said the European Union was falling behind competition in a speech Wednesday at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit.
"The EU is now losing its industrial capacity and it's losing in the competition," Putin said, according to an official English translation.
Putin used the speech to emphasize Russia's economic resilience despite U.S. sanctions, and played up opportunities for APEC members in the country, from tech to economic development.
He was the third APEC leader to speak at the summit, and followed remarks by Chinese President Xi Jinping and Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.
In his speech, Putin highlighted the country's ability to withstand a sharp drop in its U.S. dollar- and euro-denominated transactions. He also urged members to support Russia in hosting APEC in 2035.
The Russian leader is set to hold talks on Thursday with Xi and U.S. President Donald Trump in a historic meeting that could see a wide range of issues being discussed, including nuclear non-proliferation and also possibly Russia's war with Ukraine. He met with Xi on Wednesday, according to Chinese state media.
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said last week the meeting in Shenzhen would continue the efforts aimed at reaching a negotiated settlement to the Ukraine war, according to state-controlled local media Russia Today.
The summit will likely yield little concrete result, but presents an "almost 100% photo op" that lifts China's status and power at the top table, David Roche, strategist at Quantum Strategy, told CNBC's " Access Middle East " earlier this week.
— CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: NC approves Duke Energy rate hikes, new rules for data centers
articles.content_orig:
Duke Energy customers across North Carolina are facing higher electricity bills starting in January, but new rules will require large data centers to shoulder more of the financial risks associated with their growing energy demand.
After opening in downtown Raleigh one year ago, Alejandro Leon Jr., owner of Olé Sports Bar and Lounge, said a new challenge is on the horizon for his establishment: Higher electricity bills.
“We’ve been eating that up and now unfortunately with
that spike its obvious that the consumers are going to have to pay all that up
front. Very unfortunate," Leon said.
Leon says the rate hike would put business owners like himself in a crunch.
“I was pretty disappointed that North Carolina approved the
spike," Leon said.
For Durham resident Midori Brooks, who recently received a $900 electricity bill, the prospect of another rate increase means she may need to take on a second job.
Brooks has lived in the same home since 1995 and has watched her electricity bills climb. She recalls paying about $225 to $250 a month in previous years. Now, even with her husband working full time and Brooks working part time, the family is struggling to keep up.
“I have to figure out whether I'm gonna pay at least a portion of the light bill and still be able to feed my three grandkids,” Brooks said.
About $200 of her recent $900 bill was a past-due balance, she said, reflecting how difficult it has already become for her family to keep up with electricity costs even before the new rate increases take effect.
The North Carolina Utilities Commission on Monday approved two-year rate plans for Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress, largely accepting negotiated settlements that reduced the utility's original requests.
Residential electricity rates are projected to rise about 9.5% over the next two years for Duke Energy Carolinas customers and 9.3% for Duke Energy Progress customers. Duke released new figures Tuesday detailing how those increases will translate into monthly electricity bills.
The increases will begin Jan. 1, 2027, in the middle of the winter heating season.

Duke Energy Carolinas (Charlotte, Durham, the Triad and much of western North Carolina):
Duke Energy Progress (Raleigh, much of eastern North Carolina and the Asheville region):
That amounts to approximately $134 to $186 in additional annual electricity costs by 2028 for a typical household, based on Duke's projections. Actual bill impacts will vary depending on electricity usage and other charges.
Under the settlements, Duke would collect approximately $834 million in additional annual revenue across all customer classes by the second year of the rate plans.
Regulators authorized a 9.8% return on equity for both utilities, down from Duke's initial request of 10.95%. That figure represents the authorized return on shareholder equity invested in the utility, not the percentage increase in customers' electricity bills.
The rate plans include approximately $7.2 billion in capital investments over two years, along with a mechanism to refund customers for certain infrastructure projects that are delayed or canceled.
Duke also agreed to contribute a combined $20 million in shareholder funds to support electricity bill assistance and home repairs that help low-income households access weatherization programs.
Duke said it worked with customers and other stakeholders to reduce its initial rate increase requests while maintaining investments needed to strengthen the power grid and accommodate North Carolina's growth.
“We listened to our customers and worked closely with stakeholders to find a more cost-effective way forward,” said Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy's North Carolina president, in a statement Tuesday. “This outcome keeps affordability at the forefront while allowing us to make the investments needed to strengthen reliability and support North Carolina's continued growth.”
For some low-income customers, however, the financial impact could be significantly greater. A $42 monthly credit available to qualifying customers through Duke's Customer Assistance Program is scheduled to expire at the end of December, just as the new rates take effect.
Brooks said some of the programs that Durham families have relied on for help with utility bills have lost funding.
“I know I'm struggling, so I can imagine how the seniors are going to be struggling with a fixed income,” Brooks said.
The commission directed Duke to submit revised revenue calculations within 10 days of its orders and updated rate schedules for approval within 30 days.
For the first time, regulators established a separate electricity rate schedule for large data centers with power demands of at least 50 megawatts.
The decision comes as artificial intelligence and cloud computing drive unprecedented growth in electricity demand across the Carolinas.
Between March 2024 and April 2026, Duke signed contracts to provide 6.7 gigawatts of electricity capacity to new large customers in North Carolina and South Carolina. Data centers account for 92% of that contracted demand, according to the commission.
Meeting that demand will require billions of dollars in new power plants, transmission lines and other infrastructure.
Regulators found that Duke's existing and proposed billing structures did not adequately address the financial risks associated with that expansion. Without additional safeguards, other customers could be left paying for infrastructure if anticipated data center demand fails to materialize or companies leave prematurely.
New financial requirements for qualifying data center projects and expansions include:
The commission also established requirements for data centers to temporarily reduce electricity demand under certain circumstances to help maintain grid reliability.
Duke said Tuesday that regulators retained many of the company's existing data center requirements while adding financial protections intended to shield other customers from the costs and risks of serving new facilities.
Environmental advocates welcomed the new financial requirements while calling for additional measures to address the costs of generating electricity for data centers.
“This is a big step forward to ensuring that data centers pay their fair share of the costs of connecting to the grid,” said Will Scott, North Carolina policy director for the Environmental Defense Fund. “Now we need to take the next step and enable them to pay for their own new clean energy and batteries to avoid regular customers bearing the cost of unnecessary new gas plants.”
Duke indicated in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday that it is evaluating the data center provisions and will continue working with customers and other stakeholders on implementation.
Monday's rate decisions came alongside a separate ruling approving Duke's latest long-term energy plan, which extends the operation of some coal plants and calls for nearly 3,850 megawatts of new natural gas generation, alongside additional solar generation and battery storage.
The decisions come ahead of the planned merger of Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress into a single utility on Jan. 1, 2027.
Duke must now work with the Public Staff, the state agency representing utility customers, to finalize its revenue calculations before the new rates take effect.
For Brooks, the immediate concern is how to stretch her household budget even further. She is considering taking another part-time job, even if it means sacrificing time with her grandchildren.
“It's just that it's so high that you're struggling to pay because you need to keep your lights on,” Brooks said. “You gotta have your refrigerator so you can put your stuff in it. It's just heartbreaking.”

articles.title_orig: Waymo temporarily pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
articles.title_zh: Waymo temporarily pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
articles.content_orig:
Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.
The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents.
California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101.
Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco.
California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present".
In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway.
The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions".
A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance."
Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury.
Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami.
The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets.
In May, Waymo recalled thousands of its self-driving cars in the US over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads.
In the same month, multiple Waymo cars were spotted driving around a cul-de-sac in Atlanta, Georgia , in the early hours of the morning.

articles.title_orig: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
articles.title_zh: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
articles.content_orig:
At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely , a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC , CNN , Equifax , Ledger and Zoom , was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.
According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI , on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.
Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “ DarkSword ” and “ Coruna ,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.
“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote . “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”
Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”
“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”
Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.
One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.
Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds . Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.
“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”
Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “ Content Security Policies ” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.
“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”
How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.
Image: blog.report-uri.com.
The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja , which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.
Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.
“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”
Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.
Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?
“exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.”

articles.title_orig: Rare images of Indigenous group in Amazon highlight threats, advocates say
articles.title_zh: Rare images of Indigenous group in Amazon highlight threats, advocates say
articles.content_orig:
Rare images of an isolated Indigenous group emerging from a remote part of Brazil’s Amazon rainforest have highlighted the threats they face from loggers, hunters and ranchers, advocates say.
Survival International, a UK-based Indigenous rights group, shared images on Tuesday of a “historic encounter” on Monday in the northeastern state of Maranhao between a government team and about 20 uncontacted Awa people, who asked for food.
The Awa are a Tupi-Guarani people in northwestern Maranhao, some of whom remain in voluntary isolation, according to Funai, Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency.
Funai told the Reuters news agency it was reviewing videos and accounts on social media showing isolated Awa interacting with a village in the Arariboia Indigenous Land, and that the Brazilian state was not seeking contact with the group, in line with its policy of non-contact.
Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples said the encounter began on Monday near a government access control post and the village of Tawari, home to Guajajara Indigenous people, The Associated Press (AP) news agency reported. The footage was recorded by members of the Guajajara community, according to AP.
Survival International said it released the footage at the request of the Guardians of the Amazon, an Indigenous group that campaigns against illegal loggers and ranchers.
“The uncontacted Awa are under extreme pressure as intruders encroach from all sides of their territory, driving them into an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction,” said Caroline Pearce, Survival International’s director.
The Maranhao Indigenous people’s organisation COAPIMA said the encounter showed the need for careful action by the responsible agencies because of the risks that unplanned contact can pose to isolated groups , mainly from exposure to diseases.
In recent decades, isolated Indigenous groups across the Amazon have faced encroaching illegal miners, loggers and ranchers.
Contact with the groups can be deadly. In Colombia, about 40 percent of the isolated Nukak people died from diseases after outsiders reached them in the 1980s.
“If there is no forest, there are no uncontacted peoples,” Teresa Mayo, a senior researcher at Survival International, told Al Jazeera in a report on the Nukak.

articles.title_orig: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
articles.title_zh: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
articles.content_orig:
With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea
A t 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.
Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.
“We knew what the target was. Everyone was enthusiastic and excited,” one person who took part in the special operation, using the pseudonym “Leon”, told the Guardian. His 7th Deep Strike Centre is part of “Magyar’s Birds”, a brigade named after the call sign of its founder, Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces . Leon said: “Nobody gets excited any more about oil refineries. This was different.”
The soldiers got ready to launch, then watched the biplane-like drone, laden with explosives, disappear across the southern Ukrainian steppe.
Over the next four hours, hundreds of attack drones followed the same linear path, flying first over land and then over the Black Sea. In the early hours of the morning they arrived at their destination: the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia. Putin opened the monumental road and rail crossing in 2018 , driving across it in a Kamaz truck. This was four years after his undercover troops – known as little green men – seized the peninsula.
Russian propagandists had described the bridge as impregnable. It was, they said, an edifice as strong and unyielding as their country’s iron leader. For Ukraine , by contrast, it was a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Also, officials pointed out, it was illegal. Twice Kyiv had tried to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.
On this occasion, the Ukrainian military’s careful, multi-stage plan worked perfectly. “It was a well-coordinated operation. Waves of drones started from different locations. The goal was to overwhelm Russia’s well-organised air defence system, rather than the bridge itself,” Leon explained.
As expected, the initial salvo tied up Russia’s local defences. According to insiders, Ukraine then launched a second drone wave. Its function was crucial and different: to act as a relay system for radio signals. Previously, Ukrainian units had used Starshield, the military equivalent of Starlink, for mid-range strikes on occupied territory. Elon Musk’s SpaceX owns the satellite internet network, which is overseen by the Pentagon and the Trump administration.
Ten days ago, however, limits were mysteriously imposed on Ukrainian drones, so they could no longer fly at above 161 km/h (100 mph) . SpaceX insists there is no slowdown – a statement Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says is untrue . On Monday night, it appears Kyiv bypassed US restrictions by setting up its own extraordinary and innovative real-time video and radio connection.
Once the relay was in place, a third wave of attacks could begin. This time they featured Flamingos, a potent Ukrainian-made cruise missile capable of carrying 1,000kg of explosives – enough to seriously damage the bridge. An unknown number of missiles – some reports say at least four – were launched from southern Ukraine and sent towards Crimea.
A video from one of the Flamingos shows it drawing inexorably towards the target. The onboard camera captures a ghostly night-time scene. The crossing looms into view against a grisaille background. Suddenly a gigantic steel arch appears. The feed cuts out. Other footage shows the moment of impact: an orange fireball, pricking the surrounding blackness.
Photos taken on Tuesday morning in the aftermath of the attack show a scene of watery devastation. A massive arch had tumbled overnight into the Kerch straight , with a large concrete chunk of the road crossing. Nobody will be driving across the bridge anytime soon. The adjacent railway arch span was also damaged. “We were very happy, swapping messages all night,” Leon said.
One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said the timing of the operation – hailed by Zelenskyy as “unprecedented” – was deliberate. It was conducted ahead of a meeting on Thursday between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an Apec summit. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.
They added: “We understand that what we did shows the world that the king is nude. Putin is weak and vulnerable and we just proved it. The operation was purposefully designed for this specific historic moment. Putin’s plan was to bluff at the summit about how powerful he is. In reality, he can’t even protect the most important and symbolic pillars of his regime.”
In addition to Putin’s political embarrassment before his peers, the disabling of the Kerch bridge has practical consequences. Since annexing Crimea, Russia has militarised the peninsula, effectively turning it into a giant and fortified army base. Since 2022 it has been used as a launch platform for drone and missile attacks on the port of Odesa, and other Ukrainian cities in the region.
Russia’s occupying southern army has relied on the bridge for regular deliveries of ammunition, equipment and fuel. With the crossing partially closed – rail travel reportedly reopened on Tuesday – Russia will have to use an under fire land corridor instead, connecting its Rostov oblast with the Moscow-controlled parts of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces.
“We have disrupted their logistics to Crimea. There will be a lot of problems for Russia’s army in the south,” Leon predicted. Debris from the bridge strike is obstructing the narrow shipping corridor through the Kerch strait, linking the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Azov sea now resembles a lake. Passenger ferries are unable to move, with the occupied ports of Mariupol and Berdyansk cut off.
The soldiers returned from their mission jubilant and elated. Back at their headquarters, they gathered as usual for a minute’s silence, in memory of those killed in Russia’s bloody war. “We had our daily ritual as usual. Then there were congratulations on a very successful and important operation,” Leon said. Then he added: “We are paying them back.”

articles.title_orig: Hi-tech Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit
articles.title_zh: Hi-tech Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit
articles.content_orig:
Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy
I n a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping , is basking in its neon glow.
On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.
The broader Apec summit , meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.
All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.
“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”
Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.
Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.
Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.
A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.
The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.
“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”
China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”
The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.
The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”
For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”
For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo forgives person who hit him in the eye with rosary in Peru
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo forgives person who hit him in the eye with rosary in Peru
articles.content_orig:
Thankfully, the object did not hit his eye or cause serious harm.
A rosary bracelet thrown from the crowd struck Pope Leo XIV in the face Monday, just below his right eye, as he was traveling in the popemobile through the Las Palmas Air Base in Lima.
The incident occurred following a Mass at the conclusion of his apostolic trip to the country that drew nearly 1.5 million people.
Video footage shows Leo XIV ducking immediately after being hit, clearly reacting to the the impact. Thankfully, the object did not strike his eye or cause serious harm. The pope continued his journey without needing medical assistance.
Following the Mass, Pope Leo headed to the Callao Air Base, from where he departed for Rome, bringing an end to his first pastoral visit to South America as the successor of St. Peter.
Throughout his trip through Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru, the Holy Father has shown a remarkable ability to catch — on the fly — rosaries, single-decade rosaries, and other religious devotional items that the faithful often toss toward him.
Although these gestures are typically made with affection and devotion, they also entail risks, especially in large crowds and when the popemobile is moving at higher speeds.
The incident calls attention to the danger that such items being thrown at the pope can pose. What may be an expression of affection for many of the faithful can, in fact, become a risk to the physical safety of the pope and those around him.
This story was first published by EWTN News Español, the Spanish-language sister service of EWTN News. It has been translated and adapted by EWTN News English.

articles.title_orig: Beijing: China, Canada agree to 2-year extension of exemptions
articles.title_zh: Beijing: China, Canada agree to 2-year extension of exemptions
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING – China and Canada have agreed to extend relevant exemption measures under a preliminary joint arrangement on bilateral trade issues by two years, China's Ministry of Commerce said on Tuesday.
Canada will further expand exemptions for Chinese steel and aluminum products, while China will adjust anti-discrimination measures on certain Canadian agricultural and aquatic products in accordance with relevant laws and regulations, a ministry spokesperson said in response to a media query.
ALSO READ: China expands export control on precursor chemicals to US, Mexico, Canada
Guided by the important consensus reached between the leaders of the two countries, China and Canada have held multiple rounds of economic and trade consultations in the spirit of mutual respect and win-win cooperation, reaching a supplementary joint arrangement on trade issues of mutual concern, the spokesperson said.
The two sides also reached positive consensus on economic and trade issues, including e-commerce cooperation, the establishment of branches of Chinese-funded banks in Canada, and improvements to the business environment, according to the spokesperson.
READ MORE: Commerce ministry: China willing to lengthen cooperation list with Canada
The spokesperson expressed confidence that these arrangements will help deepen bilateral economic and trade cooperation and bring greater benefits to the people of both countries.
Both sides will expedite their respective domestic procedures to put the agreed measures into effect as soon as possible and continue exploring further arrangements to deepen economic and trade cooperation, the spokesperson said.
READ MORE: China and Canada agree to address EV, rapeseed issues
The spokesperson added that the two countries will make full use of the China-Canada Joint Economic and Trade Commission mechanism to expand cooperation, resolve problems, manage differences and promote the sound, stable and sustainable development of bilateral economic and trade relations.
The preliminary joint arrangement between China and Canada was reached during Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to China in January, covering trade issues including electric vehicles, steel and aluminum products, and agricultural and aquatic products.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Earnings Live Updates: First Report Since Jensen Huang’s Resignation Beats Expectations
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Earnings Live Updates: First Report Since Jensen Huang’s Resignation Beats Expectations
articles.content_orig:
The fallout from Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy as well as an Nvidia executive that led to his resignation as CEO of Nivida , the company he founded and grew into a $4 trillion chip giant, will likely go on for some time.
But the missteps of Nvidia's board of directors offer immediate lessons, say talent and leadership experts. It shows what happens when there's no clear succession plan, the dangers of an overly decentralized leadership structure, and how companies built around one powerful, controlling leader create the kind of risk boards are responsible for preventing.
In the span of less than a week — from the time Huang admitted that he was unfaithful to his wife until the board announced that he was resigning — the question became: could Nvidia, a company at the epicenter of the AI build-out, operate without him?
With Huang's ouster and the appointment of CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO , Nvidia's employees, customers, and investors will begin to find out. The process will also put a glaring spotlight on why the Nvidia board wasn't better prepared for Huang leaving the company for whatever reason.
"Succession planning is an ongoing, fundamental responsibility of the board, not something to do when a crisis hits," says Lisa Calicchio, chief human resources officer at WCG Clinical and a member of the CNBC Workforce Executive Council .
She described what happened at Nvidia as "a failure of epic proportion, both on the part of the board for not fulfilling its fiduciary responsibility to ensure continued viability of the organization by having a robust succession plan, and for the behavior and risks created by the CEO."
"What they're doing now is flying by the seat of their pants," she added.
Nvidia's 10-member board of directors is a collection of early investors, long-time partners and business executives across a range of industries. Before Nov. 12, the company did not have a chair of the board or any clear succession plan . The board also includes directors who expressed "confidence in Jensen" before they had even begun their own independent internal review of his actions.
In addition to naming Kress to the top job, the company appointed Harvey C. Jones, a tech investor and Nvidia director for the past 33 years, as its first-ever chair. After his appointment, the company announced that the board would be conducting a search of both internal and external candidates to find a permanent chief executive.
Alan Fleischmann, founder and CEO of business advisory firm Laurel Strategies and a member of the CNBC CEO Council , says that while "the DNA of any organization is defined by the CEO, there must be a stronger board dynamic and strong leadership surrounding the CEO."
"Succession planning is not simply about identifying who takes over when a CEO leaves," Fleischmann said. "It's about building an institution that can thrive beyond any one individual."
The outsized role Huang played at Nvidia — in September 2025 he told CNBC's Becky Quick that he had as many as 60 direct reports — makes it even more difficult for the board to find someone who can understand the inner workings of the company while being such a visible and active hype man for its all-important AI chips.
In corporate governance circles this is known as "key man" risk and it points to a company being overly reliant on one person whose death, departure, or financial or moral compromise could materially damage the organization.
"This is the world's most valuable company and all the risk centered on the shoulders of one man," Calicchio says.
"Flat organizations can be remarkably effective…but there are tradeoffs," Fleischmann added. "When too many decisions, relationships and reporting lines converge around one individual, the organization can become more vulnerable than it appears."
Calicchio acknowledged that a CEO having numerous direct reports isn't problematic in the early days of a company, when the founder knows everyone, but becomes concerning "when a company is the size of Nvidia. I really question the rigor and discipline of their organizational policies."
This same absence of rigor is evident in the lack of any obvious successors to Huang. "You would expect the board to have recognized at some point there was going to be an increasing need to look beyond Jensen," says Tim Wentworth, the former CEO of Walgreens Boots Alliance and Express Scripts. "This sounds so fundamental, but you don't wait for the rainy day to have the rainy day plan."
Wentworth says that when he was running both Walgreens and Express Scripts, he had a single board member assigned to each one of his direct reports so that "when we had board discussions, somebody in the room could speak about them and their strengths."
At WCG Clinical, succession and talent discussions are done quarterly, says Calicchio. "We're always looking at time frames," she says. "Is this person a definite successor, ready now, or is this someone you're grooming for the long term? Everyone wants to think that replacing the CEO is going to happen in an orderly way, but as we just saw at Nvidia, that's not always the case."
"Boards need to expect the unexpected," she adds.
Huang's powerful grip at Nvidia was great, "until it wasn't," says Wentworth. "It's really hard for a board to have a sense of urgency and the depth of intrusiveness necessary in that process when everything is going great with the company. No one wants to be the contrarian, but that's your job as a board member."

The Nikkei 225 stock index has been trading in or near bear market territory for a week and is not expected to recover its highs until artificial intelligence and data center optimism returns.
It declined 6% on Nov. 6 to close at 57,434.77, down more than 20% from a record 72,366.34 hit on June 25. A 20% fall is considered to be a technical bear market, though analysts and academics warn that a decline alone does not make a true bear market.
A landslide victory in U.S. midterm elections by the Democratic Party earlier this month rattled investors, stoking fears of a slowdown in data center construction given that many candidates pledged stricter regulations for these projects.

articles.title_orig: What is Trump hoping to achieve at APEC meeting in China?
articles.title_zh: What is Trump hoping to achieve at APEC meeting in China?
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, this week, where he is expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and hold a three-way meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
A Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the economic summit, which includes 21 Pacific Rim member economies, would be the third time the two superpower leaders have met this year.
The prior meetings – with Xi hosting Trump in Beijing in May and Trump hosting Xi at the White House in September – were heavy on ceremonial pomp, as both leaders sought to portray a sense of stability in the consequential relationship, but light on meaningful breakthroughs.
Experts predicted a similar approach in Shenzhen, as topics of AI regulation, trade and the self-ruling island of Taiwan will again loom large.
The summit comes just days after Democrats won commanding control of both chambers of the US Congress, a shift that will likely serve as a major check on the US president in his final two years in office. Beijing, meanwhile, is increasingly looking beyond the Trump era to see what comes next.
“Trump will work to strengthen his rapport with Xi, but the meeting is unlikely to produce any substantive breakthroughs,” Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser on US-China relations at Crisis Group, said.
As for Russia, Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yury Ushakov told reporters on Monday that “the significance and symbolism” of the meetings between the three superpower leaders “are hard to overestimate”.
Neither side has yet released a formal agenda for an expected Trump-Xi meeting, although the White House announced plans for the two countries to support each other at APEC and at the G20 summit in Florida in December.
“The two countries agreed to build a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity,” according to a White House statement.
As in previous meetings, AI regulation is set to loom large. Both the US and China, as industry leaders, have faced pressure to jointly agree to safeguards on the transformative technology.
In September, both sides pledged to set up a mechanism to quickly communicate AI-related incidents and to hold a dialogue on emerging risks.
Still, the Trump administration has repeatedly downplayed the need to integrate developmental guardrails. Following the White House meeting, Trump said the US would “not be putting on brakes” on the AI industry.
Speaking at a National Committee on US-China Relations event last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said both sides “expect to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before their release, and for keeping human judgment firmly in command of this technology”.
“As we do so, we should harbour no illusions about the differences between the United States and China,” he said. “And our approach to every challenge, likewise, will not always converge.”
The recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which followed revelations that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, will also loom large over any Trump-Xi meeting, even if it is not directly addressed.
Huang’s close relationship with Trump, including accompanying the US president to Beijing during his May visit, and his ties to alleged spy Alice Huang have renewed questions about the influence he exerted over the US government as he pushed to ease restrictions on the sale of advanced AI chips to Beijing.
Trump administration Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has faced particular scrutiny, including from prominent members of the Republican Party, over his reportedly lax enforcement of export controls related to China.
“Trump will be under enormous pressure from Congress and members of his own administration to raise the scandal and warn Xi that their relationship could suffer if Trump concludes that Xi has been deploying Huang and other prominent business executives to sabotage US artificial intelligence efforts,” according to Crisis Group’s Wyne.
Still, some experts expect it to have little bearing on his interaction with his Chinese counterpart.
Gabriel Wildau, managing director at the advisory firm Teneo, told Al Jazeera last week that Trump “shows no sign that he intends to disrupt the current US-China rapprochement”.
The Reuters news agency reported on Friday that US officials said Trump is not expected to raise the issue of Alice Huang with Xi.
China has denied Alice Huang was working as a spy on its behalf.
Trump has already bucked longstanding US policy on Taiwan during his recent meeting with Xi.
Following the Beijing summit in May, Trump told reporters he had discussed US arms sales to the self-governing island, which Beijing claims as its own, “in great detail” with the Chinese president.
The US has provided arms to Taiwan since 1979 as mandated under the Taiwan Relations Act. But under the 1982 Six Assurances document, Washington has not consulted with China on such sales.
In a subsequent Fox News interview, Trump also referred to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China. He has since held up approval of a $14bn arms package earmarked for the island.
The language “invites Beijing to expect something in return for each future approval”, Bonnie Glaser and Noah Munk of The German Marshall Fund of the United States (GMF) wrote in a recent analysis.
“The more successful that bargaining appears, the more Beijing will press it, and the more it will treat the next notification as a concession from Washington rather than a routine measure under the Taiwan Relations Act,” they wrote.
For its part, the White House has defended the delay, citing limited production capacity, particularly amid the US-Israel war with Iran, as well as the delicate nature of the US-China trade truce.
Democratic control of Congress, and general bipartisan support for Taiwan, could see pressure increase on the issue in Trump’s final two years in office.
“Today, the results of the midterm elections are on balance favourable for Taiwan,” Robert Sutter, a professor of international affairs at George Washington University, wrote recently for the ThinkChina publication.
Taiwan, a member of APEC, will be represented at the summit by Acer Group founder Stan Shih.
US-China trade relations took a nosedive at the start of Trump’s second term, with the US president initially launching 10 percent tariffs on China for allegedly failing to crack down on the trade of fentanyl precursors.
By April, additional US tariffs on Chinese goods had reached 145 percent , while China’s retaliatory tariffs on US goods reached 125 percent.
Agreements to bring down the temperature faltered until Trump and Xi agreed to a yearlong truce in Busan, South Korea, in October of last year. The deal was extended through January 10, 2027, following Xi’s White House visit in September.
A particular issue has been US access to China’s rare earth minerals, which was severely restricted. Still, a recent analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) found that US imports of China’s rare earth minerals during the first 11 months of the agreement remained 75 percent lower than prior to the escalation.
“The recurring challenge is the persistent gap between China’s diplomatic commitments and actual export volumes,” the analysts wrote. “Despite successive agreements in Switzerland, London, and South Korea intended to restore supplies, shipments of controlled rare earth materials to the United States remain approximately 75 percent below pre-restriction levels.”
US agricultural exports were also hard hit during the trade war, an issue for farmers that resonated during the midterm elections. In recent meetings, China has agreed to buy 25 million metric tonnes of US soya beans, as well as what the White House has described as $17bn per year in US agricultural products in 2026, 2027, and 2028.

articles.title_zh: Xiaomi 18 purportedly leaks in live image - GSMArena.com news
articles.content_orig:
Xiaomi took the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max global at an event in Paris today , and it seems like the vanilla Xiaomi 18 wants a bit of the spotlight too. A tipster on X has shared what's purportedly the first live image of the phone, which you can see below.
The white unit in the photo has a metal frame and a squircle camera island with three cameras. Unlike its Pro siblings, however, there's no secondary display on the back.
The tipster also shared the phone's expected specs, which mostly (but not entirely) line up with what leaked back in September . The Xiaomi 18 is said to have a flat 6.4-inch "1.5K" 120Hz LTPO OLED with TCL's M11 panel, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chipset, a 200MP main camera with OIS, a 50MP ultrawide, and a 50MP telephoto with OIS, along with a battery of around 7,000 mAh with 100W wired charging. It's also tipped to come with an IP69 rating, an ultrasonic fingerprint scanner, and a USB 3.2 port.
That telephoto is a bit of a departure from the September leak, which claimed the Xiaomi 18 would get a 200MP periscope with 3x optical zoom, just like the Pro models. The battery was also tipped at 7,200 mAh back then. The phone is expected to launch in China in December, so we should know for sure soon enough.

articles.title_orig: Fed official Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House firing hearing, citing bias
articles.title_zh: Fed official Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House firing hearing, citing bias
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook 's attorney on Tuesday gave the strongest signal yet that his client will not attend a hearing at the White House with a "committee of inquiry" investigating mortgage fraud allegations against Cook.
The committee established last month by President Donald Trump , who has previously tried to remove Cook from the central bank's board, is pretextual and poses a threat to the Fed, attorney Abbe Lowell wrote in a letter to presidential counsel Will Scharf.
"Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence," Lowell wrote in the letter, which is dated Monday and was made public Tuesday.
The latest correspondence came nearly two weeks after the White House committee delayed its proposed hearing with Cook to Dec. 14 from Nov. 5. Lowell said that any hearing with Cook could not take place until at least December because of conflicts with her Fed duties.
While Lowell had raised strong concerns from the outset about the legitimacy of the committee, he initially said Cook "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name."
But he has continued to cast doubts on both the committee's purpose and its composition of three executive branch officials, including National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett .
Lowell's tone sounded more hostile than ever in this week's letter, the first known to be sent by either party in the matter since the Republican Party's devastating losses in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
He accused Scharf and the committee of seeking "only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome."
Lowell highlighted two top concerns. First, he asserted that Hassett "is not competent to serve on any factfinding committee" because his prior comments about Cook "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."
Second, Lowell called it "fundamentally unfair" that the committee is demanding Cook hand over documents "immediately," while pledging to provide the governor with its own records just seven days before the hearing.
"Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote.
"Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," the lawyer wrote.
Lowell told Scharf that Cook would still be prepared to appear for a hearing if the White House "implements fair procedures." But the "ultimatums" Scharf gave in his last reply in early November "do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation," Lowell wrote.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Lowell's letter.
Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, has long sought to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden .
Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the Fed's Board of Governors, last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its meeting in September.
Trump officials sent a criminal referral last year alleging Cook may have committed mortgage fraud by falsely claiming different properties as her primary residence in order to get more favorable terms. Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing, and, after Trump tried to fire her in August 2025, filed a lawsuit to block her removal.
The Supreme Court in June prevented Trump from firing Cook, but gave him a path to try again if additional legal steps were taken. In August, the White House told Cook it was reviving its efforts to fire her on mortgage-related grounds. In October, Trump signed a presidential memo establishing the committee of inquiry to investigate allegations that Cook lied on records related to "one or more mortgage instruments."

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's Colette Kress tells Cramer: Employees and customers are not going anywhere
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's Colette Kress tells Cramer: Employees and customers are not going anywhere
articles.content_orig:
AI investors and beyond were eagerly anticipating Nvidia's ( NVDA -0.44% ) earnings call Tuesday night. The earnings report was the company's first since Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO amid controversy last week. Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress as the interim CEO as it conducts a search for a permanent replacement, considering both internal and external candidates.
Kress passed her first test with flying colors, as she delivered a confident pitch for the company and even raised guidance for fiscal 2028 from 70% revenue growth to 75% revenue growth. Nvidia also beat estimates on the top and bottom lines, and the stock was trading higher after the call, up 3.3% as of 8:23 p.m.
However, amid the focus on the headline numbers and parsing the call for hints into the company's future, there was one key comment from Kress that investors may have missed.
It's understandable why Nvidia is down a third from its peak last month, given Huang's sudden exit, but with Nvidia stock now trading at a forward P/E of just 11, the stock is as cheap as it's ever been and ripe for share buybacks.
In response to a question about the company's capital allocation and its buyback plans, Kress said that the "super top priority" for returning capital to shareholders was to use the company's current share repurchase authorization, which was raised by $150 billion in September and sat at $227.3 billion at the end of the third quarter. Kress added, "So thinking about all of that together, I think there is definitely room to continue all of the stock repurchase plans that we want to do and complete those before the end of fiscal year '28." She also noted that the top priority for its capital spending is supporting its suppliers in building out additional capacity.
If Nvidia executes on those buybacks and the stock price stays roughly the same, it would reduce shares outstanding by roughly 6% by Jan. 2028, when fiscal 2028 ends.
The share repurchase authorization and Kress's commitment are a positive sign, not just because it will lift Nvidia's earnings per share, but because it shows management's confidence that the stock is undervalued after the recent sell-off and signals to investors that it's worth buying.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/17/26
For investors worried that Nvidia would struggle during the transitional period, Kress gave no indication that anything has changed, saying, "it's business as usual," and that customers, suppliers, and partners are all "100% behind us."
Demand for the company's products continues to outstrip supply, and Kress spent much of the call reiterating the company's commitment to securing adequate supply, which allowed it to raise its revenue guidance for fiscal 2028.
In just one quarter, its supply commitments increased from $279 billion, primarily due to memory supply. Kress said, "We feel confident in terms of both the demand that we have in front of us as well as the supply and additionally that we can do the 75%," referring to 75% revenue growth next year.
Nvidia also addressed the controversy around Jensen Huang, and new Chairman of the Board Harvey Jones made it clear that the board has no intention of reinstating Huang. Regarding the CEO search, Jones said, "We want to install this CEO, the permanent CEO, as quickly as possible, but we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person." Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, who has been seen as a possible replacement for Huang, was on the Q&A portion of the call, but did not answer any questions.
Nvidia did what it needed to do on the earnings call and then some. Its commitment to using up its $227 billion share repurchase authorization and the guidance hike for fiscal 2028 show investors the company continues to excel. Nvidia is on track to bring in more than $700 billion in revenue next year. Given the deep discount, Nvidia looks like a buy , even without Jensen Huang.
